summary: Describes how to use Transport Layer Security to protect Common Open Policy Service (COPS) connections. It also updates RFC 2748 by changing the contents of the Client-Accept message. It is a standards-track memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4261 describes how to run COPS, the protocol that hands network policy to devices, over TLS. The policy server and the device start as they normally would, then one of them asks for a TLS handshake by putting a small extra object in its first message. After the handshake, the policy itself is encrypted and both ends check each other's certificates.

questions: how to secure cops with tls
how does cops start a tls handshake
what is the integrity tls object in cops
subtitle: How a policy server and its devices upgrade a plain COPS connection to a TLS-protected one.

tldr.problem: COPS protects the integrity of policy as it travels hop by hop, but some organizations need the policy itself to be confidential, for example when policy crosses domain boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a COPS object, Integrity-TLS with C-Num 16 and C-Type 2, that either side puts in a Client-Open or Client-Accept message to start a TLS handshake on the same port as plain COPS.
tldr.outcome: Once the handshake is done, all COPS messages travel as TLS application data, with the same certificates and cipher suite rules as any TLS deployment. RFC 4261 was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4261 was published in December 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8996, which brings the TLS requirements up to date. The document also updates RFC 2748, changing the contents of the Client-Accept message.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
COPS was designed to distribute clear-text policy information from a centralized Policy Decision Point (PDP) to a set of Policy Enforcement Points (PEP) in the Internet. COPS provides its own security mechanisms to protect the per-hop integrity of the deployed policy. However, the use of COPS for sensitive applications, for example some types of security policy distribution, requires additional security measures, such as data confidentiality. This is because some organizations find it necessary to hide some or all of their security policies, for example because policy distribution to devices such as mobile platforms can cross domain boundaries.

TLS was designed to provide channel-oriented security. TLS standardizes SSL and may be used with any connection-oriented service. TLS provides mechanisms for one-way and two-way authentication, dynamic session keying, and data stream privacy and integrity.

This document describes how to use COPS over TLS, abbreviated COPS/TLS. It also updates RFC 2748 by modifying the contents of the Client-Accept message.

The document's glossary names COPS as the Common Open Policy Service, COPS/TCP as a plain-vanilla implementation of COPS, and COPS/TLS as a secure implementation of COPS using TLS. The PDP is the Policy Decision Point, also referred to as the Policy Server, and the PEP is the Policy Enforcement Point, also referred to as the Policy Client.
sections.plainLanguage: COPS sends policy in the clear, with its own checks that the policy was not altered on the way. This document adds encryption on top, so that the policy itself cannot be read.

sections.title: Separate Ports versus Upward Negotiation
sections.content:
There are two ways in which insecure and secure versions of the same protocol can be run simultaneously.

In the first method, the secure version of the protocol is also allocated a well-known port. This strategy of having well-known port numbers for both the secure and insecure versions is known as Separate Ports. The clients requiring security can simply connect to the well-known secure port. This method is easy to implement, with no modifications needed to existing insecure implementations. The disadvantage, however, is that it does not scale well, because a new port is required for each secure implementation. More problems with this approach have been listed in RFC 2595.

The second method is known as Upward Negotiation. In this method, the secure and insecure versions of the protocol run on the same port. The client connects to the server, both discover each other's capabilities, and start security negotiations if desired. This method usually requires some changes to the protocol being secured.

In view of the many issues with the Separate Ports approach, the authors of RFC 4261 decided to use the Upward Negotiation method for COPS/TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: You could give the secure version its own port number, or you could run both on one port and let the two ends agree to switch to encryption. This document picks the second, because a new port for every secure variant does not scale.

sections.title: The Integrity-TLS Object
sections.content:
The TLS Integrity object is used by the PDP and the PEP to start the TLS negotiation. It should be included only in the Client-Open or Client-Accept messages, and it MUST NOT be included in any other COPS message.

The object is laid out as a Length field of 16 bits, then C-Num set to 16 and C-Type set to 2, then a reserved 16-bit field that is set to zero and should be ignored on receipt, and finally a 16-bit Flags field. Flag 0x01 is StartTLS, which indicates that the sender of the message wishes to initiate a TLS handshake.

The Client-Type of any message containing this object MUST be 0. Client-Type 0 is used to negotiate COPS connection level security and must only be used during the connection establishment phase.

IANA has added the C-Num and C-Type combination 0x10 and 0x02 for the Integrity-TLS object to the COPS parameters registry, and for Client-Type 0 the Flags value 0x01 for StartTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The object is a small header, a reserved area and a 16-bit flags field. Only one flag is defined, and setting it says that the sender wants to start a TLS handshake.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
The document uses the error codes described in section 2.2.8 of RFC 2748, the Error Object.

Error code 13 is Unknown COPS Object. Sub-code octet 2 contains the unknown object's C-Num, and octet 3 contains the unknown object's C-Type. If the PEP or PDP does not support TLS, the C-Num specified MUST be 16 and the C-Type MUST be 2. This demonstrates that the TLS version of the Integrity object is not known. This error code MUST be used by either PEP or PDP to indicate a security-related connection closure if it cannot support a TLS connection for the COPS protocol.

If the PDP wishes to negotiate a different security mechanism than the one requested by the PEP in the Client-Open, it MUST send error code 15, Authentication Required. Sub-code octet 2 contains the C-Num=16 value for the Integrity Object, and octet 3 MUST specify the PDP's required or preferred Integrity object C-Type. If the server does not support any form of COPS-Security, it MUST set octet 2 to 16 and octet 3 to zero instead, signifying that no type of the Integrity object is supported.

IANA has recorded the sub-code meanings for error code 15: octet 2 is the C-Num of the Integrity object and octet 3 is the C-Type of the supported or preferred Integrity object, or zero. The two registered combinations are 15 with octet 2 set to 16 and octet 3 set to 0, meaning no security, and 15 with octet 2 set to 16 and octet 3 set to 2, meaning Integrity-TLS supported or preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Two error codes matter here. One says the other end has never heard of this TLS object, the other says the server wants a different kind of protection than the client asked for. The sub-code says which kind.

sections.title: Secure Connection Initiation
sections.content:
Security negotiation may be initiated by either the PDP or the PEP. The PEP can initiate a negotiation via a Client-Open message, while a PDP can initiate a negotiation via a Client-Accept message. Once the TLS connection is established, all COPS data MUST be sent as TLS application data.

When the PEP initiates, it MAY start a TLS security negotiation with a PDP using the Client-Open message. To do this, the Client-Open message MUST have a Client-Type of 0 and MUST include the Integrity-TLS object. Upon receiving it, the PDP SHOULD respond with a Client-Accept message containing the Integrity-TLS object. The contents of the Client-Accept message defined in section 3.7 of RFC 2748 need not change, except that the C-Type of the integrity object contained there should now be C-Type=2. The new format of the Client-Accept message does not replace or obsolete the existing format, which can continue to be used for non-secure COPS session negotiations. Upon receiving the appropriate Client-Accept, the PEP SHOULD initiate the TLS handshake.

In case the PDP does not wish to open a secure connection with the PEP, it MUST reply with a Client-Close message and close the connection, including error code 15 with octet 2 set to 16 and octet 3 set to the C-Type of the server's preferred Integrity type, or zero for no security. A PEP requiring the Integrity-TLS object in a Client-Accept message MUST close the connection if the object is missing, sending the same error code 15 with octet 3 set to 2.

When the PDP initiates, the PEP initially opens a TCP connection with the PDP on the standard COPS port and sends a Client-Open message with a Client-Type of 0. The PDP SHOULD then reply with a Client-Accept message, and to signal the PEP to start the TLS handshake the PDP MUST include the Integrity-TLS object in that message. Upon receiving it, the PEP SHOULD initiate the TLS handshake, and if for any reason it cannot, it MUST close the connection. After receiving the Client-Accept, the PEP MUST NOT send any messages until the TLS handshake is complete. Upon receiving any message from the PEP before the TLS handshake starts, the PDP MUST issue a Client-Close message with error code 15.

A PDP wishing to negotiate security with a PEP that has an existing non-secure connection MUST send a Client-Close with error code 15, with octet 2 set to 16 and octet 3 set to 2, and then wait for the PEP to reconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Either end can ask for the upgrade. The request travels in the first message of the connection, and the answer comes back in the second. After that the two ends run the TLS handshake and everything else is sent inside it.

sections.title: Connection Closure
sections.content:
TLS provides facilities to securely close its connections. Reception of a valid closure alert assures an implementation that no further data will arrive on that connection. The TLS specification requires TLS implementations to initiate a closure alert exchange before closing a connection. It also permits TLS implementations to close connections without waiting to receive closure alerts from the peer, provided they send their own first. A connection closed in this way is known as an incomplete close. TLS allows implementations to reuse the session in this case, but COPS/TLS makes no use of this capability.

A connection closed without first sending a closure alert is known as a premature close. A premature close does not call into question the security of the data already received, but simply indicates that subsequent data might have been truncated. Because TLS is oblivious to COPS message boundaries, it is necessary to examine the COPS data itself, specifically the Message header, to determine whether truncation occurred.

PEP implementations MUST treat premature closes as errors and any data received as potentially truncated. A PEP system detecting an incomplete close SHOULD recover gracefully. PEP systems SHOULD send a closure alert before closing the connection. PEPs unprepared to receive any more data MAY choose not to wait for the PDP's closure alert and simply close the connection, which generates an incomplete close on the PDP side.

COPS permits a PEP to close the connection at any time and requires PDPs to recover gracefully. PDPs SHOULD be prepared to receive an incomplete close from the PEP, since a PEP often shuts down for operational reasons unrelated to the transfer of policy information. PDP systems MUST attempt to initiate an exchange of closure alerts with the PEP system before closing the connection, and MAY close the connection after sending the closure alert, generating an incomplete close on the PEP side.
sections.plainLanguage: Closing a TLS connection properly means sending a closing message first. If the other end just vanishes, the data that arrived may have been cut short, and the COPS message header is what tells you so.

sections.title: Endpoint Identification and Access Control
sections.content:
All PEP implementations of COPS/TLS MUST support an access control mechanism to identify authorized PDPs. This requirement provides a level of assurance that the policy arriving at the PEP is actually valid. PEP deployments SHOULD require the use of this access control mechanism for operation of COPS over TLS, and when access control is enabled the PEP implementation MUST NOT initiate COPS/TLS connections to systems not authorized as PDPs by that mechanism.

Similarly, PDP COPS/TLS implementations MUST support an access control mechanism permitting them to restrict their services to authorized PEP systems only, although deployments MAY choose not to use one at the PDP, as organizations might not consider the types of policy being deployed as sensitive. If access controls are used, the PDP implementation MUST terminate COPS/TLS connections from unauthorized PEP systems and log an error if an auditable logging mechanism is present.

Implementations of COPS/TLS MUST use X.509 v3 certificates conforming to RFC 3280 to identify PDP and PEP systems, and MUST perform certificate verification processing conforming to RFC 3280. If a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName or iPAddress is present in the PDP's certificate, it MUST be used as the PDP identity. If both types are present, dNSName SHOULD be used. If neither type is present, the most specific Common Name field in the Subject field of the certificate SHOULD be used.

When PEP systems are not access controlled, the PDP does not need external knowledge of what the PEP's identity ought to be, so checks are neither possible nor necessary. There is no requirement for PEP systems to register with a certificate authority, and COPS over TLS uses one-way authentication, of the PDP to the PEP. When PEP systems are access controlled, PEPs MUST be the subjects of end entity certificates, COPS over TLS uses two-way authentication, and the PDP MUST perform the same identity checks for the PEPs as for the PDP.

All PEP implementations MUST provide a mechanism to securely deliver or configure the bootstrap policy that identifies the PDPs the PEP is authorized to connect to, and MUST be able to securely acquire the trust anchor for each authorized Certification Authority that issues PDP certificates. They MUST also support a mechanism to securely acquire an access control list or filter identifying the set of authorized PDPs associated with each CA.

If the PDP hostname or IP address is available via the bootstrap policy, the PEP MUST check it against the PDP's identity as presented in the PDP's TLS Certificate message. If the bootstrap policy identifies the authorized PDP only by an IP address, the subjectAltName MUST be present in the certificate and MUST include an iPAddress format matching the expected name. If the hostname of the PDP does not match the identity in the certificate, a PEP on a user-oriented system MUST either notify the user or terminate the connection with a bad certificate error. PEPs on unattended systems MUST log the error to an appropriate audit log and MUST terminate the connection with a bad certificate error.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends use X.509 certificates. The device checks that the server is the one it was told to expect, and may also check that only approved servers are contacted at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
A COPS PDP and PEP MUST check the results of the TLS negotiation to see whether an acceptable degree of authentication and privacy have been achieved. If the negotiation has resulted in unacceptable algorithms or key lengths, either side MAY choose to terminate the connection.

A man-in-the-middle attack can be launched by deleting the Integrity-TLS object or altering the Client-Open or Client-Accept messages. If security is required, the PEP and PDP bootstrap policy must specify this, and PEP and PDP implementations should reject Client-Open or Client-Accept messages that fail to include an Integrity-TLS object.

On cipher suites, implementations MUST support the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher suite. All other cipher suites are optional.

The PEP and PDP SHOULD be backward compatible with peers that have not been modified to support COPS/TLS, and SHOULD handle errors generated in response to the Integrity-TLS object.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the handshake is done, both ends should check that the result is acceptable, because an attacker could have removed the request for encryption altogether. One cipher suite is mandatory; the rest are optional.
